title: Bidirectional BFS in Singapore: Meeting in the Middle ⚡
description: Watch a real-map style pathfinding demo in Downtown Core where two BFS waves start at the start and goal simultaneously. When they meet, the algorithm reconstructs the shortest route with far fewer node visits than standard BFS.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — How launching two simultaneous searches doubles graph traversal speed ⚡

In this Singapore (Downtown Core) visualization, we run BFS from BOTH ends: 
• Forward BFS expands from the start. 
• Backward BFS expands from the destination (on the same unweighted graph). 
• The moment the frontiers intersect, we’ve found the shortest path and stop early.

Technical breakdown (why it’s faster):
If the shortest path length is d and the branching factor is b, classic BFS explores ~O(b^d) nodes. Bidirectional BFS reduces this to roughly O(b^(d/2) + b^(d/2)) ≈ O(b^(d/2)), because each side only needs to “grow” halfway. That’s the “meeting in the middle” graph optimization you use in interviews.

Takeaway: Same shortest-path guarantee as BFS, but dramatically fewer expansions in practice.

Debate question: In your coding interviews, when would Bidirectional BFS beat plain BFS—and when might it be less convenient due to graph representation or directionality?
